description: PIRX stands for Planetary Intelligence & Research eXploration. We are a team driven by curiosity, technology, and a passion for space. Our goal is to explore real-world challenges through research, data, and creative problem-solving. We believe great ideas start with asking the right questions, working together, and turning what we learn into practical solutions that can make a difference both on Earth and beyond.
summary:
We developed PIRX, a web application that helps people explore and understand wildfire activity using NASA FIRMS satellite data from MODIS and VIIRS. Users can select an area on the map, view fire detections, compare different months and years, and understand whether the activity is higher or lower than the historical average.

Our project addresses the challenge by turning complex satellite data into a simple and interactive tool that people can actually use. We also keep the data sources and processing history clear, so the results are easier to trust and reproduce.

This is important because wildfire information can be difficult to understand, especially when it comes from different satellites and large datasets. PIRX can help researchers, communities, and decision-makers explore fire patterns and learn more about changes in their environment.
details:
In our project, we built PIRX, a web application that helps people explore wildfire activity using NASA FIRMS satellite data. The application uses MODIS and VIIRS data and displays fire detections on an interactive map. Users can choose an area, filter the results by date or satellite, view individual observations, and compare fire activity with historical patterns.

The main challenge we addressed was making complex satellite data easier to understand and use. PIRX can help researchers, students, communities, and decision-makers learn more about wildfire activity and environmental changes. We used Python, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, PostgreSQL with PostGIS, MapLibre, ECharts, and Docker to build the project.

The creative part is that we brought maps, charts, historical calendars, satellite comparisons, and data-source information together in one platform. We also considered missing data, differences between satellites, uncertainty, accessibility, performance, and making sure the results are not presented as exact fire-risk predictions.
